content: Epidemiological transition refers to a shift in the predominant patterns of disease within a country, moving from infectious diseases to degenerative diseases. This concept was first introduced by Omran in 1971. The transition typically occurs as a country undergoes modernization or economic development. In less economically developed countries, infectious diseases are more prevalent due to lower standards of medical care. In contrast, in more economically developed countries, infectious diseases such as cholera and typhoid are effectively managed and treated. As a result, people live longer and are more likely to die from degenerative diseases, such as cancers and cardiovascular conditions. There are generally two recognized epidemiological transitions. The first transition occurred when human societies shifted from hunting and gathering to primary food production. This change led to an increase in infectious and parasitic diseases due to the emergence of new vectors and vehicles of disease transmission. The second epidemiological transition took place in modern times, characterized by the control of infectious diseases and a rise in chronic, non-infectious, degenerative diseases. This second transition is most commonly observed in wealthy, industrialized nations, often referred to as first-world countries. In contrast, third-world nations continue to experience a higher burden of infectious diseases compared to chronic diseases.
